Agriculture investment forum seeks P1 billion private funds
Jasper Emmanuel Arcalas - The Philippine Star
March 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said they plan to entice private sector investments into the sectors of cacao, mango, seaweed and coffee through the DA’s first-ever national investment forum.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Agriculture (DA) is seeking to secure at least P1 billion of investments from the private sector in its upcoming national investment forum, where it will showcase some of its key commodity priorities.
Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said they plan to entice private sector investments into the sectors of cacao, mango, seaweed and coffee through the DA’s first-ever national investment forum.
The forum is centered on the United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)’s hand-in-hand initiative wherein countries present investment proposals that might be attractive to global investors.
“We want to grow these four industries as soon as possible so they need investments both coming from local and foreign,” Tiu Laurel said on the sidelines of the launching of the national investment forum yesterday at the Asian Development Bank.
“We see the huge potential of these commodities in the international and domestic markets. We want to grab the opportunity to export more. So, we need private sector investments,” he added.
Dulce Carandang, FAO assistant representative to the Philippines, said the hand-in-hand initiative seeks to accelerate transformation of nation’s agriculture and food systems through targeted investments.
These investments, Carandang pointed out, help improve farmers’ welfare, make food production more resilient to climate crisis, boost economic development and fight hunger and poverty.
Tiu Laurel said the national investment forum aims to promote agriculture as a “highly” bankable sector despite it being one of the most vulnerable to climate threats.
“We want to bridge the global capital and local stakeholders,” he said.
“Through this forum, we redefine Philippine agriculture from being a legacy of the past to a sustainable engine for growth,” he added.
The DA noted that the hand-in-hand initiative links data-driven agricultural priorities with financing and technical expertise.
Andrew Jeffries, ADB country director for the Philippines, said some of the country’s decades-old policies have limited income and development in the country’s farm sector.
For ADB, some of the priority investment areas in agriculture are climate change and disaster, modernizing agricultural value chains and improving nutrition, Jeffries said.

A Cambodia-linked investment group has outlined plans to invest in commercial properties and develop new business links in regional South Australia, with a focus on hospitality, recycling, agricultural exports and workforce training.
The plans were presented at the “Study, Work & Investment in South Australia” forum at The Morgan Tower in Phnom Penh on September 26. Rasmey Sokmongkol, known as Raz, is managing director of AIA-SA and leads the Flinders Investment Group (FIG), the investment consortium behind the proposed property developments.

A booklet prepared for the forum says FIG plans to invest in four commercial properties across Jamestown, Georgetown and Gladstone in South Australia’s Mid North. The group has identified possible uses for the buildings, but the materials do not state whether acquisitions have been completed. No investment value, financing details or development timetable was disclosed.
Four properties identified for redevelopment
FIG’s property plans centre on buildings that could be renovated for accommodation, hospitality and other commercial uses:
 Jamestown: The Old Belalie Hotel and a former Farmers’ Co-operative Union building.
 Georgetown: A general store and adjoining four-bedroom home.
 Gladstone: A former butter factory.
At the Old Belalie Hotel, the booklet proposes renovating existing rooms to provide accommodation for visitors, temporary workers and new residents. It also raises the possibility of modular housing on adjacent land. The former co-operative building in Jamestown is presented as a potential site for a new dining business.
In Georgetown, FIG’s proposed approach includes renovating the home beside the general store and potentially adding guest rooms. Together, the projects reflect the group’s view that regional businesses need more accommodation options to support tourism and incoming workers.
The investment case presented in the booklet extends beyond the individual buildings. The Yorke and Mid North region has a population of more than 78,000 and includes agricultural areas, established service centres and transport links, according to the forum materials. FIG sees an opportunity to connect renewed commercial properties with the region’s existing industries and future workforce needs.
Recycling, exports and tourism in focus
AIA-SA’s wider strategy includes plastics and glass recycling in the Mid North. The group said it is developing a “weighed and paid” collection model through warehouse and logistics operations, with the aim of handling materials at greater volume. The forum materials did not specify the planned processing capacity or when operations would begin.
Trade is another priority. AIA-SA said it is working with a Mid North wine company and Clare Valley producers to develop export channels for South Australian wine and primary produce into Southeast Asian markets. The materials did not name buyers or disclose expected export volumes.
The group also wants to acquire and upgrade regional hospitality assets, particularly around the Yorke Peninsula, to attract visitors and create local employment. These plans remain at the proposal stage in the materials provided.
FIG was described as an investment consortium founded by Sokmongkol alongside Cambodian business figures. A photograph in the forum report identifies its members as Chea Sunsopor, Sokmongkol, Chea Leanghong and Lai Porhour.
Training linked to regional business activity
AIA-SA also presented international education as part of its regional strategy. Through allied frameworks including the Australian Training and Education Centre, it said it is working with accredited training organisations in construction, English, tourism and hospitality.
The aim is to connect students with practical learning opportunities alongside commercial sites and warehouse operations in regional South Australia. The group did not provide student targets, details of individual training agreements or a timetable for placements.
For Sokmongkol, the South Australian focus has a personal connection. The forum report says he arrived in Adelaide as a refugee and attended school there before moving into international business development.
The report also described discussions with Andrew “Cosi” Costello, a South Australian television personality and founder of Cows for Cambodia, about a possible ambassadorial role promoting the Yorke Peninsula and Mid North. It did not say that a formal appointment had been made.
The Phnom Penh forum put a range of cross-border opportunities on the table. The next measure of progress will be whether FIG completes its proposed property investments and provides firm funding, construction and operating plans for the businesses it wants to build.

Archer Aviation (ACHR) Raises $650M, Moves to Buy Hawthorne Airport for $126M; Shares Slip After Q3 Update — Nov. 7, 2025
by Mateusz Kaczmarek
7 November 2025
Archer Aviation Inc. (NYSE: ACHR) unveiled a multi‑pronged update tied to its third‑quarter results: a $650 million equity raise, a deal to acquire control of Los Angeles’ Hawthorne Airport for $126 million, fresh flight‑test milestones for its Midnight eVTOL, and the closing of its Lilium patent portfolio purchase. The stock traded around $8.88 mid‑day as investors digested the capital raise and airport plan. (
What happened today
 Archer to acquire control of Hawthorne Airport (HHR) for $126M. The company signed definitive agreements to gain control of the 80‑acre field (Jack Northrop Field) just under three miles from LAX. Archer says Hawthorne will anchor its planned Los Angeles air‑taxi network and serve as an AI operations testbed, including AI‑powered traffic and ground‑ops management. The transaction remains subject to closing conditions and city approval. (
 Structure matters: Archer is assuming the master ground lease, not buying the land outright. The ground lease with the City of Hawthorne runs through 2055, and the company lists additional capital projects planned at the site as part of an “airport of the future” build‑out. (
 $650M primary equity raise. Archer filed a 424B5 prospectus supplement for 81,250,000 new shares priced at $8.00 per share (gross proceeds $650M). After the issuance, total Class A shares outstanding are listed at ~732.5 million. A separate prospectus covers up to ~$27.6M of additional shares to settle a contractual payment in stock. (
 Q3 2025 highlights. GAAP net loss was $129.9M; adjusted EBITDA loss was $116.1M. Archer reported $1.64B in cash, cash equivalents, and short‑term investments at quarter‑end and guided Q4 adjusted EBITDA loss to $110–$140M. (
 Flight‑test and IP milestones. Midnight completed a 55‑mile piloted flight (31 minutes, >126 mph) and a 10,000‑ft altitude flight; Archer also closed the Lilium patent portfolio acquisition, taking its global IP assets to >1,000. (
Why Hawthorne matters
HHR’s location—near LAX, SoFi Stadium, the Intuit Dome, The Forum, and Downtown LA—makes it a strategic hub for short‑hop urban missions Archer is targeting ahead of the LA28 Olympic Games. Industry coverage notes the airport is slated to be the central node of Archer’s LA network and a staging area for 2028 operations, subject to approvals. (
Important fine print: Archer emphasizes it will assume the master lease (not purchase the land), with lease renewal risk and capex obligations to transform the site. The company also flags execution and certification risks in the prospectus. (
Certification & production: where things stand
Archer says it is largely through Phase 3 of the FAA type‑certification program and is focusing on Phase 4 (implementation and formal TIA testing). The company estimates it has received ~15% of compliance verification documents in that final phase. Archer also notes it holds a Part 135 air carrier certificate and is producing six Midnight aircraft across U.S. facilities for testing, certification, and non‑U.S. launch‑edition programs. (
Internationally, Archer highlights test and demonstration flights in the UAE and new airline partnerships in Korea (Korean Air) and Japan (JAL/Soracle JV), with some agreements still conditional. (
The market’s read so far
 Stock reaction: ACHR traded near $8.88 mid‑day Friday after the update (see live chart above). Early headlines framed premarket softness around investor debate over the airport deal and ongoing cash burn. (
 Analysts:JPMorgan cut its price target to $8 (Neutral) after the Q3 print; Needham reiterated Buy but trimmed its target to $10. (
 Flows:ARK Invest disclosed buying over 3 million ACHR shares on Nov. 6 across multiple funds, according to portfolio‑tracking outlets and financial media. (
By the numbers (Q3 and recent moves)
 Equity raised:$650M via 81.25M shares at $8.00 (primary registered direct). Shares outstanding post‑deal: ~732.5M. (
 Cash & investments:$1.64B at Sept. 30, 2025 (liquidity now > $2B with the new raise, per company). (
 P&L:GAAP net loss $129.9M; adjusted EBITDA loss $116.1M. Q4 adj. EBITDA guide: loss of $110–$140M. (
 Hawthorne Airport:80 acres; ~190,000 sq ft of facilities; <3 miles from LAX; AI testbed designation. Acquisition of control via master lease assumption pending city approvals; lease through 2055. (
 Technology/IP:>1,000 global IP assets after Lilium patent purchase (≈300 assets). (
 Flight tests: Longest piloted flight 55 miles (31 min); top altitude 10,000 ft. (
Context: Archer’s LA ambitions and airline ties
Archer has been building a Los Angeles network blueprint, with LA28 Olympics ties previously announced in mainstream coverage. The company also keeps close airline partnerships (e.g., United Airlines) for integrating urban air mobility into existing air networks. (
Industry outlets underscore how pinning a near‑LAX base could streamline airport‑to‑city eVTOL trips—the core, high‑frequency routes urban air mobility depends on—while providing Archer a controlled environment to trial AI‑enabled operations at scale. (
What to watch next
1. City of Hawthorne approvals & closing of the airport transaction; specifics on capex and redevelopment timeline at HHR. (
2. Equity issuance settlement and any subsequent updates on capital allocation (the 424B5s outline both the $650M primary and a separate stock‑for‑services issuance). (
3. FAA certification cadence (transition into TIA testing within Phase 4) and Production Certificate progress. (
4. International ramp, including UAE launch‑edition activities and the Korean Air/Japan partnerships once definitive terms are finalized. (
5. Analyst and fund flows as markets recalibrate on dilution, execution at HHR, and certification timelines. (
Reporting notes & sources

 SEC filings (Nov. 6–7, 2025):424B5 for 81.25M shares @ $8.00 and separate 424B5 for stock in lieu of cash payments; details on lease structure, lease term to 2055, certification progress, and risk factors. (

 Ryan Lawler

Audeo Ventures, an early-stage firm that invests in regulated and infrastructure-heavy markets, is nearing a final close on its $70 million Fund II, its co-founders tell Axios exclusively.
Why it matters: Many emerging managers are getting squeezed as LPs consolidate commitments with fewer, more established funds.
Context: The co-founders — Greg Laurent Josi and Pavel Tinkov — started their careers in hedge funds and public markets before moving into venture.
 They began investing in private companies in 2020, founded Audeo in 2021, and raised a roughly $20 million Fund I to back startups they were already tracking.
Between the lines: Audeo began Fund I by writing about $500,000 to $1 million checks, but shifted to a more concentrated approach, including one position that is about 35% of the fund.
 The founders say Fund II will start with average checks of about $2.5 million to $3.5 million in the first few years, then double- and triple-down on winners.
 "To stand out in this game, you need to take concentrated positions," Tinkov says.
Zoom in: Audeo's early portfolio includes bets in fintech and consumer finance, such as Plata, Rosaly and Jackpot.com.
 The firm has had two major exits in X1's acquisition by Robinhood and Caramel's acquisition by eBay.
State of play: Audeo began raising Fund II in January last year and hit its initial $50 million target in four to five months, the founders say. They later raised the target to $70 million.
 Fund II currently sits at about $65 million in confirmed commitments and is about a month from closing, they add.
 They say Fund II's LP base has shifted from mostly personal connections to single-family offices, multi-family offices and "quasi-sovereign" entities, with an emphasis on adding more institutional LPs over time.
The big picture: Tinkov says the 2022 to 2024 lull in fintech investing was "a blessing in disguise" because larger funds stepped back, allowing smaller firms to gain access to deals.
 Now that the market has picked up, the founders argue their public markets background keeps them disciplined on valuations and fundamentals, even when deals get hot.
What's next: Audeo says it expects to deploy more than 70% of Fund II in the U.S., with Latin America as a secondary focus.
 The founders have been based mostly in Dubai during fundraising, but Tinkov plans to move to the Bay Area, while Josi plans to move to New York to be closer to investment opportunities.
